input: This example considers a continuous stirred-tank reactor running a hydrolysis that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.144 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time is 23 min, and on the basis of these figures the steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR works out at 76.8%. It is helpful to be clear about what lies behind that figure. In an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor, the contents are assumed to be perfectly mixed, which means that the composition is uniform throughout the vessel and identical to the composition of the stream leaving it, and consequently the reaction proceeds everywhere in the vessel at the rate corresponding to the outlet concentration. Since the reaction is first order, that rate is the lowest rate anywhere in the system, because the reactant concentration is at its lowest at the outlet, and it is this rate that, combined with the residence time, determines the conversion that the balance over the vessel produces. The estimate does, however, rest on assumptions that deserve to be noted. It assumes perfect mixing and constant density, and while constant density is a relatively mild assumption in this context, perfect mixing is a stronger one, and it has not in fact been verified on the actual vessel, because tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. In a real vessel, bypassing or stagnant regions could allow part of the feed to pass through with considerably less reaction than the ideal calculation suggests. Overall, then, the figure of the ideal-vessel conversion should be read as the conversion that the stated kinetics and residence time would deliver under ideal conditions, rather than as a guaranteed prediction of the performance of the actual equipment.
target:
Steady-state conversion for the hydrolysis in an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor is 76.8%. The reaction is first order in the limiting reactant, the rate constant is 0.144 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time is 23 min.

An ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor is perfectly mixed, so the composition everywhere in the vessel equals the outlet composition, and the reaction proceeds throughout the vessel at the rate set by that outlet composition. The conversion then follows from a steady-state balance over the whole vessel: the rate at which the limiting reactant leaves in the outlet stream, together with the rate at which it is consumed by reaction, balances the rate at which it enters. Because the reaction is first order, the rate falls as the reactant is consumed, and the rate that governs the balance is the lowest in the system, the rate at the outlet concentration. Residence time sets how long the reacting mixture is exposed to that rate, and the stated conversion is the joint result of the two stated quantities under the ideal-mixing assumption.

The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density. Constant density fixes the residence time at its stated value, since the volumetric flow through the vessel then matches the flow the residence time was computed from. Perfect mixing is the stronger assumption, and it is unverified on the actual vessel: tracer tests have not been run, so the residence-time distribution is not measured. Bypassing or stagnant zones in a real vessel would let part of the feed leave with less reaction than the ideal figure states. The conversion is therefore the ideal-vessel result for the stated rate constant and residence time, and a measured conversion on the actual vessel stands as a separate quantity until the mixing assumption is tested.
